title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Overview: objects against the wind
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. A wind tunnel moves air past a stationary object so engineers can measure what flight would do to it. Tunnels span the speed ladder from vacuum — where air is so thin that molecules rarely collide — up through subsonic, transonic, supersonic, and hypersonic flow. The object under test can be any shape: spheres, cylinders, flat plates, cones, full airfoils, even complete vehicle models, and modern tests include multi-material surfaces like ablative heat shields whose texture changes as they burn. Every run records the same core story: how much drag the shape makes, how much lift, where the flow separates, and how heat loads the surface.
capabilities: The speed ladder: vacuum, subsonic, transonic, supersonic, hypersonic
What every run measures: drag, lift, separation, heating
Shape families under test, from spheres to full vehicles
Multi-material surfaces and why texture matters

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Subsonic wind tunnels
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Subsonic tunnels test at Mach numbers below 0.8, where air behaves nearly incompressibly. Closed-circuit tunnels recirculate the same air through a loop, saving energy; open-circuit tunnels draw fresh air in and exhaust it. Famous examples include the NASA Ames 40-by-80-foot tunnel, large enough to test full aircraft. Because the model blocks part of the test section, engineers apply blockage corrections to the measured drag, and wall interference corrections account for the tunnel walls squeezing the flow. Reynolds number matching — testing at the same ratio of inertial to viscous forces as real flight — matters more than matching speed exactly.
capabilities: Open-circuit vs closed-circuit tunnel designs
NASA Ames 40-by-80: full-scale subsonic testing
Blockage and wall-interference corrections
Reynolds number matching between model and flight

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Transonic and supersonic tunnels
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Near Mach 1 the flow goes transonic: pockets of supersonic flow appear over wings, ending in shock waves that add wave drag. Transonic tunnels use ventilated walls — slots or perforations — so the shocks reflect less and the choked flow does not lock the test section. Supersonic tunnels (Mach 1.2 to 5) accelerate air through converging-diverging nozzles; once the throat chokes, the diverging section expands the flow past Mach 1. Schlieren photography makes the shock diamonds and bow shocks visible as light bends through density gradients. Run times can be short — blowdown tunnels exhaust a high-pressure tank in seconds to minutes.
capabilities: Transonic shock formation and wave drag
Ventilated walls: slotted and perforated test sections
Converging-diverging nozzles for supersonic flow
Blowdown tunnels and short run times

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Hypersonic tunnels and shock tubes
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Above Mach 5 the air itself starts to change: molecules dissociate, ionization begins, and the heat loads demand exotic facilities. Hypersonic wind tunnels use arc-jet heaters or combustion to reach thousands of degrees; shock tubes and expansion tubes fire a shock wave down a long pipe to create milliseconds of true hypersonic flow for scramjet and reentry research. Ludwieg tubes — long pressurized pipes with a fast valve — give clean, quiet hypersonic flow for boundary-layer transition studies. At these speeds the test is as much about surviving the heat as measuring the forces.
capabilities: Mach 5+ flow: dissociation, ionization, extreme heating
Arc-jet facilities for heat-shield testing
Shock tubes and expansion tubes: milliseconds of true hypersonic flow
Ludwieg tubes for quiet transition research

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Vacuum and rarefied flow: from vacuum upward
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. From vacuum upward means starting where there is almost no air at all. In rarefied flow the Knudsen number — the ratio of molecular mean free path to object size — decides the physics: below 0.01 the air acts as a continuum and normal aerodynamics apply; from 0.01 to 0.1 slip flow begins at the surface; from 0.1 to 10 the flow is transitional; above 10 molecules hit the object one at a time in free-molecular flow. Vacuum chambers with molecular beam sources test satellite drag and thruster plumes in true space-like conditions, bridging the gap between pure vacuum and the first breathable continuum.
capabilities: The Knudsen number and the four flow regimes
Free-molecular flow: satellites and upper-atmosphere flight
Vacuum chambers with molecular beam sources
Bridging vacuum to continuum in one database

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Shape drag data catalog
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Real measured drag coefficients, the dimensionless numbers that let one shape be compared to another: a smooth sphere measures about 0.47 in subsonic flow; a long cylinder across the flow about 1.17; a flat plate facing the wind about 1.28; a streamlined body of revolution as low as 0.04. Cones trade drag for stability at supersonic speeds, and airfoils are catalogued by lift curve slope and stall angle rather than drag alone. The database records each shape with its reference area definition, Reynolds number, Mach number, and surface finish — because a drag coefficient without its conditions is just a rumor.
capabilities: Sphere 0.47, cylinder 1.17, flat plate 1.28, streamlined body 0.04
Reference area definitions that make coefficients comparable
Reynolds and Mach conditions attached to every value
Airfoil records: lift slope, stall, and polar curves

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Multi-material surface records
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Real vehicles wear many materials at once: ablative heat shields like PICA char and erode during reentry, tiles sit beside blankets beside metal structure, and each junction trips the boundary layer differently. Surface roughness moves transition — the point where smooth laminar flow becomes turbulent — forward, raising both drag and heating. Wind tunnel records capture this by testing panels that mix materials, measuring heat flux with coaxial thermocouples and infrared cameras, and photographing the char pattern after the run. A heat shield is tested the way it flies: burning.
capabilities: Ablative heat shields: PICA char and erosion in the tunnel
Mixed-material panels: tiles, blankets, and structure together
Roughness-driven boundary layer transition
Heat flux measurement: thermocouples and infrared imaging

title: The Wind Tunnel Shapes Database — Measurement instruments
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Wind tunnel instruments turn air into numbers. Strain-gauge force balances — mounted inside the model on a sting — resolve lift, drag, and moments to fractions of a percent. Pressure taps, tiny holes plumbed to scanners, map the pressure distribution that the pressure coefficient summarizes. Particle image velocimetry fires laser sheets through seeded flow and tracks particle displacements between frames to map velocity fields. Schlieren and shadowgraph optics visualize density gradients and shocks; hot-wire anemometers measure turbulence by how fast the flow cools a heated wire.
capabilities: Sting-mounted strain-gauge force balances
Pressure taps and the pressure coefficient
Particle image velocimetry: laser-sheet velocity fields
Schlieren optics and hot-wire turbulence measurement
